name: Emeka Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal lineworker shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew for an electricity company, building new spans and repairing damaged power lines. We start with the truck and the isolation sheet; after a storm, half my time is deciding which pole and which crew should go first. I have a two-year technical diploma, though the best lesson for a young worker is watching someone stop when a plan is wrong. My partner and I have two children at school and a mortgage, so I try to keep a few months of expenses set aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that a little AI in the depot can help sort routine forms. I use a tool now and then to draft a stock request, but a lineworker still checks the actual damaged part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our typical pay and a few months saved make the mortgage manageable if shifts stay steady. I would not call AI a threat in this picture, though a wrong stock request can delay a repair. A broken crossarm does not become the right bracket because an AI stock request looks tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present crew rota and check each drafted stock request against the damaged part before sending it. In the first year I would continue putting seventy from any paid storm callout into the family emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work, with the usual care over bills. A small tool saving minutes at the depot does not change how I lead a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part gets confused in a stock request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A broken crossarm and its bracket can look like one order line in a quick summary. I read the measurements from the field sheet before asking the store for either part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no storm callout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I do not make the seventy transfer that month. We keep the usual mortgage payment and use the savings already there only when needed.

say: **Small** AI tools may help stock requests while crews still check damaged line parts.
I would **keep** site measurements ahead of any generated order.
think: **Typical** wages and several months of savings make steady shifts workable for our mortgage.
A **wrong** bracket order can waste repair time even when AI change is mild.
do: **Keep** crew rota and compare drafted stock requests with field measurements.
**Save** seventy from each actual paid storm callout.
feel: **Calm** about lineworker income while remaining careful with family bills.
S0.quote: A broken crossarm does not become the right bracket because an AI stock request looks tidy.
fieldNote: His **occasional** AI use is a clerical aid checked against physical measurements.
The **family** cushion supports calm, while extra saving depends on actual paid storm work.

steps.text: Keep crew rota and verify stock requests against field measurements
Save seventy from each paid storm callout into emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say stronger AI could make buying and booking quicker, but I would want the crews involved in judging the new stock lists. A planner can order a bracket; a field worker must tell whether it fits the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office staff shrink, stores may get less human checking and our crew could spend more unpaid time chasing parts. I do not expect line repairs to vanish now, but losing callout time would slow the savings we build for the children. A parts list earns my trust one repaired power line at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for access to the new parts tool and learn its error-report button on paid time. During the first year I would compare ten AI stock lists with what our crew used, show the store manager the differences and keep a record of any lost callout time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about how the workflow changes, though willing to try a tool that proves itself. I would be calmer if reports from field crews actually changed the lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you report through the error button?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would report the pole type, bracket size and work order where the list is wrong. Then I would ask the store manager to show me whether the next list was corrected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the store manager ignores your ten comparisons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the record and bring it to our regular depot safety meeting. I would not tell the crew to trust a list that keeps sending the wrong parts.

say: I would **learn** the parts tool and test stock lists against ten real repairs.
**Field** reports must be able to correct buying mistakes.
think: **Office** shrinkage may leave fewer people checking orders and more wasted crew time.
**Lost** callout hours would weaken savings for the children even if line jobs remain.
do: **Learn** the paid-time error-report function in the parts tool.
**Compare** ten AI stock lists with actual crew parts and report errors.
**Record** any lost callout time during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about workflow changes but open to evidence from a trial.
S1.quote: A parts list earns my trust one repaired power line at a time.
fieldNote: He **adopts** a new AI function when he can test it on real parts and report errors.
He **worries** about lost callout time, not immediate replacement of the field crew.

steps.text: Learn parts tool error-report function on paid time
Compare ten AI stock lists against actual line repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that full thinking AI by 2028 could make the stock and dispatch decisions, with capable line robots around 2031. I would ask the company to test a robot on damaged poles with a paid crew watching, not only in a clean yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years between the thinking tool and the robot would go quickly. If robots take a large share of storm callouts, our mortgage is still payable for a few months from savings, but losing that income for longer would hurt the family. Three months of savings can buy time for a lineworker; it cannot buy back every storm callout a robot takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for the written plan for paid robot field trials and put one hundred more from each monthly wage into emergency savings. In the first year after 2028 I would take a paid trial shift if the crew can stop the machine; I would also compare the actual pay of the few nearby lead openings if callouts start falling. On that paid trial shift I would learn the robot controls before touching a live repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not helpless. I would rather have the pay figures and a chance to test the machine than spend three years guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the machine on a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If its grip damages a crossarm or it reaches beyond the isolation boundary, I would stop the trial. The crew’s authority would need to be written down before I accepted the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether another job is worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the written wage, callout rules and travel time with this job. I would not move my children’s school for a vacancy notice with no offer.

say: **Thinking** AI could control stock and dispatch by 2028, while line robots follow around 2031.
I would **accept** paid field trials only with crew stop authority.
think: A **large** storm callout loss could outlast our few months of savings.
Our **mortgage** and children make the actual pay of nearby roles important.
do: **Save** one hundred extra from each normal monthly wage this year.
**Take** a paid robot field trial shift after 2028 if crew can stop it.
**Compare** nearby lead pay only if callout hours begin falling.
feel: **Anxious** about longer income loss, with figures and trial conditions offering some control.
S2.quote: Three months of savings can buy time for a lineworker; it cannot buy back every storm callout a robot takes.
fieldNote: He **treats** robot testing as paid work with explicit stop authority, not passive observation.
**New** monthly saving comes from normal pay, while local job comparison depends on callout decline.

steps.text: Save one hundred extra monthly from normal wages
Learn robot controls on paid field trial after 2028 if crew can stop work
Compare nearby lead jobs if callout hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that 2031 for thinking AI and 2034 for line robots gives time to set proper fault tests. I would want the apprenticeship program to include a machine plan that an apprentice is allowed to challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep earning as a crew lead while becoming the person who checks robot repair plans. Some nearby companies might need that skill, but I would first want proof that my electricity company pays for the training and actually uses the role. An apprentice should be allowed to catch the wrong robot bracket before a line crew fits it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company this year for its robot oversight course syllabus, paid hours and any posted lead vacancy. If it funds hands-on training and posts a role at no lower wage, I would enroll before 2031 and apply when the vacancy opens; if not, I would stay with my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, yet the years let me decide from real tests. I can learn a proved method without tossing away a sound trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the oversight course show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a damaged line, wrong bracket and failed isolation marker in the exercises. A course that only teaches where to tap approval would be useless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stay with the same company first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My crew knows my calls and I know the network. I would only compare another employer’s written offer if our company had no paid path or cut our lead hours.

say: The **extra** years allow apprentices to challenge robot plans before line deployment around 2034.
I would **support** oversight training built on real faults.
think: A **robot** oversight role could preserve my earnings if paid training and a genuine vacancy exist.
I **prefer** proven methods and known crews before a speculative employer move.
do: **Request** course syllabus, paid hours and posted lead vacancy details this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if hands-on course is funded and suitable post appears.
**Apply** for posted oversight role only if wage is no lower than current pay.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to test a paid path before changing roles.
S3.quote: An apprentice should be allowed to catch the wrong robot bracket before a line crew fits it.
fieldNote: His **willingness** to train rests on physical fault examples and written job terms.
He would **keep** the current crew if paid training or a suitable post does not appear.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if hands-on course funded and suitable role posted
Apply for posted oversight role if wage meets current pay
Keep power line crew lead shifts if no paid path appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade before thinking AI and about three more years before line robots gives us time to keep the old apprenticeship strong. A robot should be checked by workers who know why a drawing can be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I may choose fewer storm nights, but I cannot assume a retirement date or a paid teaching place. A decade would let us work down the mortgage if our wages hold, then decide what hours fit the family. A robot display can name the bracket; a lineworker still has to measure the damaged pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask my partner to set a monthly mortgage overpayment we can actually afford and begin with sixty from normal wages. In the first year after 2036 I would keep leading repairs, then apply for a posted paid apprentice supervisor opening only if its hours and salary cover our remaining mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about my job with that much lead time. I would still expect each generation to learn from the damaged line, not just the robot display.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the sixty is too much one month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would skip that extra payment and make the regular mortgage payment first. I would not borrow for the sake of a neat savings target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a new apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put a real field measurement beside the robot’s proposed bracket and ask which one fits. If the apprentice cannot explain it, the crew is not ready to trust the machine.

say: A **decade** lets the company keep practical apprenticeships before capable robots arrive around 2039.
**Workers** must still compare machine plans with field measurements.
think: **Future** storm hours and mortgage balance are uncertain, so a teaching post is optional.
I **want** paid work at suitable hours, not an assumed early retirement.
do: **Pay** sixty extra on the mortgage from normal monthly wages when affordable.
**Keep** leading repairs after thinking AI arrives in 2036.
**Apply** for posted paid apprentice supervisor role if salary and hours fit mortgage.
feel: **Fairly** calm with time to reduce debt and judge future work.
S4.quote: A robot display can name the bracket; a lineworker still has to measure the damaged pole.
fieldNote: He **favours** apprenticeships and small new debt payments over a promised retirement.
His **supervisor** option depends on an actual posted opening with workable pay and hours.

steps.text: Pay sixty extra monthly on mortgage when normal wages allow
Apply for posted paid apprentice supervisor role if salary covers mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the line robots could reach storm repairs around 2031 before our crew knows what happens to callout pay. A paid field trial with a written stop rule and clear notice about hours would help. I can work with a robot plan after I have seen it fail safely on a real pole.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the store and field crews get to correct the AI parts lists together. A wrong bracket does not care which department bought it. My young workers need to know why the real measurement wins.

headlineQuote: I can work with a robot plan after I have seen it fail safely on a real pole.
portrait: **Emeka** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and a habit of measuring damaged parts before ordering.
**Typical** pay and one to six months of savings support his partner, two school-age children and mortgage.
He **uses** AI occasionally, adopts tools after field proof, and wants paid crew authority over robot trials.
He could **train** for a funded oversight role or later supervise apprentices, while keeping current shifts until real offers exist.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031 before storm callout pay and safety rules are clear.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** field trials with a written stop rule and early notice of hour changes would help him prepare.
